Australian hospitality workers strike disrupts restaurants and hotels nationwide

SYDNEY, June 12 — Thousands of hospitality workers across Australia walked off the job on Wednesday, leading to widespread disruptions at restaurants, cafes, and hotels as negotiations over pay and conditions stalled.

The walkout, organized by the United Hospitality Workers Union, began early morning and affected major cities including Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane, and Perth. Industry groups estimate at least 1,200 venues, ranging from luxury hotels to family-run restaurants, have been forced to either close or operate with limited services as staff joined picket lines.

"We have been left with no choice but to take action," said union spokesperson Carla Nguyen at a rally outside the Grand Pacific Hotel in Melbourne. "Our members are demanding a fair wage and safer working conditions. Many have been working understaffed for months with no adequate compensation."

At Sydney’s Bayshore Restaurant, owner Michael Tan said regular service was impossible with only a handful of workers crossing the picket line. "We’ve had to cancel lunch and dinner bookings for the next two days," he said. "We support our staff’s right to protest, but this situation is putting enormous strain on our business."

Industry analysts estimate the strike could cost the sector up to A$15 million per day in lost revenue if it continues through the weekend. The Australian Hospitality Association urged both sides to return to the negotiating table. "The industry is still recovering from the challenges of the past few years. Prolonged action will hurt businesses and workers alike," said AHA President John Ritchie.

Union leaders said the strike would continue until employers make a "meaningful offer" on wage increases and improved rostering practices. Talks between the union and the National Hospitality Employers Council are scheduled to resume Thursday.

Many hospitality workers remained on picket lines late Wednesday, chanting for better pay and conditions as customers faced shuttered doors and empty dining rooms.
